en.case.starbem.title: From Pandemic Response to Scalable Digital Health Platform
en.case.starbem.overview.company: Starbem is a Brazilian healthtech focused on providing accessible digital healthcare services. The platform connects patients with healthcare professionals — including doctors, psychologists, psychiatrists, and nutritionists — with a strong emphasis on mental health solutions for companies (B2B).
en.case.starbem.context.title: Context
en.case.starbem.context.p1: During the COVID-19 pandemic, access to healthcare became limited and overwhelmed. People faced uncertainty about symptoms, when to seek emergency care, and how to safely access medical support.
en.case.starbem.context.p2: In this scenario, we identified an opportunity to leverage telemedicine to provide fast, reliable, and scalable medical assistance — reducing the burden on healthcare systems and guiding patients with clarity.
en.case.starbem.context.p3: As demand grew and the model was validated, the MVP evolved into Starbem, a robust digital health platform that became a reference in corporate healthcare in Brazil.
en.case.starbem.challenge.label: Challenge
en.case.starbem.challenge.intro: The main challenge was to design and launch a solution that could quickly diagnose, triage, and guide patients.
en.case.starbem.challenge.research: Research revealed critical barriers of access and communication that needed to be solved in real time:
en.case.starbem.challenge.list.1: Lack of clear guidance for patients with COVID-19 symptoms
en.case.starbem.challenge.list.3: Low accessibility to immediate medical support
en.case.starbem.challenge.conclusion: The challenge was to ensure trust, usability and scalability in a high-uncertainty environment — validating quickly without compromising experience quality.
en.case.starbem.process.label: Process
en.case.starbem.process.intro: The project followed an accelerated discovery, validation and delivery cycle, adapted to the pace required by the pandemic context.
en.case.starbem.process.step1.title: Research
en.case.starbem.process.step1.desc: Early-stage research with affected users to understand behaviors, fears, and needs in a crisis context.
en.case.starbem.process.step2.title: Journeys
en.case.starbem.process.step2.desc: Defined key user journeys focused on symptom triage and decision-making.
en.case.starbem.process.step3.title: Alignment
en.case.starbem.process.step3.desc: Facilitated alignment sessions with stakeholders and partners, defining scope and success criteria.
en.case.starbem.process.step4.title: Prototyping
en.case.starbem.process.step4.desc: Led rapid prototyping cycles to validate assumptions. Conducted usability tests to refine flows and reduce friction.
en.case.starbem.process.step5.title: Delivery
en.case.starbem.process.step5.desc: Collaborated closely with cross-functional teams for fast iteration, MVP launch, and continuous product evolution.
en.case.starbem.decisions.label: Decisions
en.case.starbem.decisions.intro: One of the first strategic advantages of the project was access to a large database: more than 120,000 people had already been assisted through Missão Covid. However, the first challenge was turning that volume of data into reliable insights.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p1: We selected a sample of 2,000 people, but only 177 responded, representing approximately 9% of the sample. Rather than treating the low response rate as a blocker, we used the available data together with qualitative research and benchmarking to identify clear patterns and validate our assumptions.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p2: One of the most important findings was related to the target audience. The research showed that 77% of respondents from lower-income classes did not have a health insurance plan, reinforcing an opportunity to create a more accessible healthcare solution. Combined with benchmark analysis, we identified R$19.90 as a viable entry price, helping us narrow the initial target and define a clearer business proposition.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p3: Initially, the product had been conceived to serve all social classes. The research challenged this assumption. Instead of trying to build a product for everyone, we used evidence to focus the MVP on a more specific audience: people who needed accessible healthcare and were less likely to have traditional health insurance.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p4: The qualitative research then helped translate these strategic decisions into product requirements. Conversations with doctors and patients challenged some of our initial assumptions, particularly around video consultations and the different needs of each user. Doctors needed a web experience that allowed them to access medical information and exams more efficiently, while patients needed a simpler and more convenient mobile experience.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p5: Another important decision came later in the process. Even after the main functional requirements had been defined, we realized that the product still looked too similar to Missão Covid. Although the functionality was evolving, the product identity had not yet been established.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p6: I saw this as an opportunity to act beyond the initial wireframing scope. While the team continued working on flows and use cases, I took ownership of the visual direction and began co-creating a new identity in parallel. I developed the first concepts and presented different directions to the CEO and product founder. Through several iterations and discussions, we moved away from the original concept and arrived at the name Starbem and its new visual identity.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p7: Once the direction was fully aligned, the team incorporated the new identity into the product and we progressed toward the final prototype.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p8: The MVP was launched in 2021 with approximately 3,000 active customers, entering the market with a product proposition grounded in research, validated assumptions, and a clearly defined target.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p9: What started as a pandemic response evolved into a scalable business. Over the following years, the business model expanded from B2C to B2B, and by 2023 Starbem had reached 230,000 active users. The company was subsequently separated from our original structure to continue operating independently.
en.case.starbem.decisions.p10: For me, the most important outcome of this project was not simply creating the interface. It was demonstrating how research, data, qualitative insights, benchmarking, and design decisions could transform uncertainty into a clearer product strategy — turning real user pain points into business opportunities and helping an MVP evolve into a scalable digital health product.
en.case.starbem.gallery.label: Project
en.case.starbem.strategy.p1: I acted strategically across the entire product lifecycle — from discovery to delivery — leading a multidisciplinary team and translating complex user pain points into actionable product opportunities.
en.case.starbem.strategy.p2: I identified that over 60% of patients did not know when to seek emergency care, which caused both overload at emergency rooms and underreporting of severe cases. The core problem was not just clinical — it was about communication, trust, and access.
en.case.starbem.strategy.p3: To solve this, I proposed a telemedicine MVP centered on three experience pillars:
en.case.starbem.strategy.item3: reliable guidance between home recovery and emergency referral.
en.case.starbem.strategy.p4: I also identified gaps in the onboarding journey and in the platform's value communication — especially in the B2B market. I restructured the flow to ensure companies could quickly understand the product's impact on their employees' health.
en.case.starbem.strategy.p5: I aligned stakeholders around a clear product vision, conducted rapid validation cycles to reduce risks, and built the foundation that allowed the product to evolve from an emergency MVP into a scalable digital health business.
en.case.starbem.strategy.p6: As a result, this approach transformed an emergency response initiative into a long-term solution — connecting user experience with revenue growth, B2B expansion, and investor attraction.

en.case.pernambucanas.title: Scaling Design to Enable a Phygital Ecosystem
en.case.pernambucanas.overview.company: Pernambucanas is one of the largest retail chains in Brazil, recognized as a phygital company for seamlessly integrating physical stores with digital experiences. With a strong presence in retail and financial services, the company has been evolving its ecosystem to deliver more connected, efficient, and user-centered solutions.
en.case.pernambucanas.context.title: Context
en.case.pernambucanas.context.p1: I joined Pernambucanas at an early stage of its UX maturity, when design was still emerging as a discipline within the organization. Over time, I evolved into a Design Coordinator, leading a team of 12 designers across multiple business units and playing a key role in the company's digital transformation.
en.case.pernambucanas.context.p2: My journey followed the shift from design evangelization to strategic enablement, helping structure teams, processes, and ways of working to support a growing and complex product ecosystem.
en.case.pernambucanas.context.p3: My trajectory reflected the evolution of a company that transformed design from an operational function into a strategic driver of customer value delivery.
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.label: Challenge
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.intro: The main challenge was to scale design across a fragmented and complex environment.
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.research: The ecosystem was composed of multiple Business Units with distinct business rules, technologies, and back-end systems. As a result:
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.list.1: Lack of consistency across products and journeys
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.list.2: Disconnected experiences between physical and digital channels
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.list.3: The need to accelerate delivery without compromising quality
en.case.pernambucanas.challenge.conclusion: The goal was to transform this complexity into a cohesive, scalable, and user-centered experience ecosystem.
en.case.pernambucanas.process.label: Process
en.case.pernambucanas.process.intro: The design process was refined into an adaptable structure to support different business contexts, focused on clarity, team autonomy, and strategic alignment.
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step1.title: Kickoff
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step1.desc: Alignment sessions with stakeholders to define goals, expectations, and scope for each initiative across BUs.
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step2.title: Discovery
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step2.desc: Internal interviews and research to map business rules, existing flows, and improvement opportunities.
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step3.title: Prototyping
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step3.desc: Workflow planning and collaborative prototyping with product, engineering, and business teams.
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step4.title: Validation
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step4.desc: Usability testing with real users to validate hypotheses and refine flows before delivery.
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step5.title: Iteration
en.case.pernambucanas.process.step5.desc: Continuous refinement cycles aligned with business goals, monitoring implementation and product evolution.
en.case.pernambucanas.gallery.label: Project
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.p1: I acted as a strategic design leader at Pernambucanas during a critical transformation moment: design needed to move from execution to decision-driving — capable of connecting multiple business units around a coherent and scalable experience.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.p2: The ecosystem's fragmentation exposed a structural problem: each Business Unit operated with its own rules, technologies, and design processes — generating visible inconsistencies in the customer journey and reducing team delivery capacity.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.p3: To address this, I organized the work around three strategic pillars:
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.item1: Team structure — building and scaling design squads across 6+ BUs, with complementary roles and product culture.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.item2: Process & operations — implementing an adaptable design workflow that harmonized different contexts without losing delivery speed.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.item3: Experience system — evolving the Design System as a consistency layer between digital and physical, standardizing without rigidity.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.p4: The launch of Pernambucanas' first digital account was a strategic milestone: it required integration across retail, financial services, and technology, with design as the connective thread across journeys. I led the end-to-end process — from scope definition to real-user validation.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.p5: In parallel, I structured design leadership as an enablement function: 1:1s, career development plans, mentoring, and alignment rituals that strengthened team autonomy and design culture across the organization.
en.case.pernambucanas.strategy.p6: The result was the transformation of complexity into competitive advantage — with a more cohesive phygital ecosystem, more mature teams, and an omnichannel experience capable of connecting physical and digital channels around the customer journey.

en.case.pernambucanas.impact.intro: Strategic design leadership delivered concrete digital transformation milestones, strengthening Pernambucanas' phygital ecosystem and expanding its presence in financial services.

en.cases.daycoval.desc: Transforming the Pix experience in the app.
en.case.daycoval.title: Transforming the Pix experience at Banco Daycoval
en.case.daycoval.overview.label: About the Bank
en.case.daycoval.overview.company: Banco Daycoval is one of Brazil's leading financial institutions, with strong operations in credit, payroll loans, treasury and financial solutions for individuals and companies. With roughly 2.3 million customers, the bank is among the largest in the country and is going through a moment of digital evolution, investing in modernizing its products and in the maturity of its user experience processes.
en.case.daycoval.overview.fact1.label: Industry
en.case.daycoval.overview.fact2.label: Platforms
en.case.daycoval.overview.fact3.label: My role
en.case.daycoval.overview.fact3.value: UX Specialist — Product Design, UX Research and Discovery
en.case.daycoval.context.title: Context
en.case.daycoval.context.p1: My role at Banco Daycoval is broad, connecting different business areas to turn user needs into opportunities for the digital products. I work daily in partnership with Business, Product, Technology, Security and Compliance teams, acting as the link between customer needs and the company's strategic goals.
en.case.daycoval.context.p2: When I joined the bank, my main goal was to strengthen the UX culture and raise the maturity of the Design and Product processes. To do so, I implemented structured research, discovery and validation practices, creating processes that allowed the team to make evidence-based decisions rather than relying only on perceptions.
en.case.daycoval.context.p3: During this period I structured the Usability Testing process, developing standardized scripts, support materials, evaluation criteria and tools to monitor sessions, using Maze for moderated and unmoderated research with real customers.
en.case.daycoval.context.p4: I also strengthened the research practice by creating Benchmark templates, best practices for market analysis and documentation of key learnings. As a next step, I began structuring a consistent Desk Research process, making research a continuous pillar within the team.
en.case.daycoval.context.p5: In parallel, I took part in evolving different app features such as Checking Account, Credit Card and, above all, Pix, a strategic feature for the bank.
en.case.daycoval.context.p6: The challenge of this project was to modernize the entire Pix experience while respecting the technical, regulatory and operational constraints of the existing environment. Since the implementation would run across different development tracks, we needed a solution that allowed gradual evolution without compromising the customer experience.
en.case.daycoval.context.p7: As a strategy, we started the redesign by creating a Pix Home, establishing a new architecture to organize the whole feature. This decision also gave rise to a broader strategy for the app: letting each major feature have its own home page, better organizing user journeys and easing the product's future evolution.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.label: Challenge
en.case.daycoval.challenge.intro: The main challenge was to evolve one of the most important features of the app while balancing innovation, technical constraints and regulatory rules already established by the bank.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.research: In addition, the implementation would happen gradually, requiring new flows to coexist with features already live in production, without creating inconsistencies for users. The main challenges identified were:
en.case.daycoval.challenge.list.1: Evolving a critical feature without compromising the current experience.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.list.2: Reconciling existing business rules with new opportunities identified during research.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.list.3: Aligning expectations across Product, Business, Technology, Security and Compliance.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.list.4: Deeply understanding the existing flows before proposing changes.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.list.5: Building a scalable architecture for future app features.
en.case.daycoval.challenge.list.6: Ensuring the implementation could happen incrementally.

en.case.daycoval.process.label: Process
en.case.daycoval.process.intro: The project followed a structured flow of research, validation and delivery, connecting discovery, evidence and development follow-up.
en.case.daycoval.process.step1.title: Research and understanding
en.case.daycoval.process.step1.desc: Immersion to understand the current state of Pix within the bank, with internal research, stakeholder interviews and mapping of the main pain points from customers and business areas.
en.case.daycoval.process.step2.title: Benchmark and opportunities
en.case.daycoval.process.step2.desc: Comparative analysis of leading banks and fintechs to identify patterns, opportunities and best practices, guiding product decisions and strategic discussions.
en.case.daycoval.process.step3.title: Ideation and prototyping
en.case.daycoval.process.step3.desc: Solutions built with the Product and Design teams in collaborative ideation and Design Critique sessions, with technical alignments to validate feasibility before testing.
en.case.daycoval.process.step4.title: Validation and alignment
en.case.daycoval.process.step4.desc: Presentations to Business and stakeholders sharing learnings from research, benchmarks and usability tests. The feedback refined the solution before development.
en.case.daycoval.process.step5.title: Handoff and follow-up
en.case.daycoval.process.step5.desc: Handoff to the development team, documenting interface specifications, component behavior and business rules, with implementation follow-up to ensure consistency.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.label: Decisions
en.case.daycoval.decisions.intro: One of the most challenging moments of this project was balancing the insights from user research with the expectations of the business areas.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.p1: During the redesign of the Pix limits management experience, usability tests showed that customers struggled to understand the number of available options and, in many cases, did not clearly grasp how the limits worked. However, the initial expectation from the leadership was to keep the existing structure, as it was aligned with the bank's established rules and processes.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.p2: Rather than simply following that direction, I sought to gather more evidence to support a more consistent decision. I worked together with the Pix product owner, the Security team and other areas involved to understand the feature's technical, regulatory and operational constraints. In parallel, I used the benchmark results to show that leading banks were simplifying limit configuration, reducing the number of options and making the experience more intuitive.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.p3: This discussion involved several areas, including Product, Business, Technology, Security and Compliance. Several alignment rounds were needed, since an apparently simple interface change directly impacted internal Pix rules, services and implementation flows.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.p4: Throughout these conversations, it became clear that the best solution would not be to serve only the business vision or only the research results, but to find a balance between user needs and the bank's constraints. Together with the Product team, we evaluated different alternatives until we reached a proposal that reduced the journey's complexity without compromising regulatory and operational requirements.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.p5: As a result, we delivered a simpler experience, with fewer interactions for the customer, aligned with the standards of the market's leading players and ready to evolve in a scalable way.
en.case.daycoval.decisions.p6: More than redesigning a feature, this project reinforced the importance of using research, benchmarks and data as instruments to influence decisions and build consensus across areas. In a highly regulated environment such as the financial sector, the project's success depended not only on the quality of the proposed solution, but also on the ability to communicate its value and engage all stakeholders around the same vision.

en.cases.pefisa.desc: Analysis of 4 digital accounts and a proposal to unify them into a single app.
en.case.pefisa.title: Strategy for Unifying B2B Digital Products
en.case.pefisa.overview.company: Pefisa is the financial arm of the Pernambucanas group, responsible for the ecosystem's financial services: cards, credit and the Digital Account. Its technology platform powers not only Pefisa's own account but also partner solutions such as Pernambucanas, Leroy Merlin and Palmeiras Pay.
en.case.pefisa.context.title: Context
en.case.pefisa.context.p1: Pefisa faced high technology costs from maintaining two Digital Account solutions in parallel: a native app and a white-label version.
en.case.pefisa.context.p2: The core goal of the analysis was to compare the existing solutions and propose a migration or restructuring plan, considering performance, user experience and usability.
en.case.pefisa.context.p3: The outcome must guide the company's digital strategy for the medium and long term, with a recommendation backed by data, not preference.
en.case.pefisa.challenge.label: Challenge
en.case.pefisa.challenge.intro: The main challenge was to decide which platform to keep across four products that shared the same technology but evolved independently.
en.case.pefisa.challenge.research: Pefisa, Pernambucanas, Leroy Merlin and Palmeiras Pay ran on two separate codebases. As a result:
en.case.pefisa.challenge.list.1: Duplicated maintenance cost to ship the same features
en.case.pefisa.challenge.list.2: Redundant features and inconsistent experiences across apps
en.case.pefisa.challenge.list.3: A scattered roadmap, with team effort split across multiple fronts
en.case.pefisa.challenge.conclusion: The challenge was to build an objective analysis framework that compared the solutions and pointed to the path with the greatest potential for scale and centralization.
en.case.pefisa.gallerymosaic.label: Gallery
en.case.pefisa.gallerymosaic.intro: The analysis slides: feature mapping, scores per pillar, the comparison across accounts and the unification proposal.
en.case.pefisa.process.label: Process
en.case.pefisa.process.intro: The evaluation was built on three pillars: Performance, Experience and Usability, consolidated into a proposal and an implementation roadmap.
en.case.pefisa.process.step1.title: Performance
en.case.pefisa.process.step1.desc: Technical interviews with the engineering team, critical bug assessment and average app response time.
en.case.pefisa.process.step2.title: Experience
en.case.pefisa.process.step2.desc: Analysis of NPS metrics and review of user feedback on Google Play and the App Store.
en.case.pefisa.process.step3.title: Usability
en.case.pefisa.process.step3.desc: Heuristic evaluation and comparative feature mapping across the four solutions.
en.case.pefisa.process.step4.title: Proposal
en.case.pefisa.process.step4.desc: A unification recommendation built on the best-performing solution, absorbing the strengths of the others.
en.case.pefisa.process.step5.title: Roadmap
en.case.pefisa.process.step5.desc: Phased implementation plan, with feature prioritization alongside the project sponsor and technical detailing with the Engineering team.
en.case.pefisa.project.label: Project
en.case.pefisa.project.title: Technical assessment
en.case.pefisa.project.desc: In the technical interviews, each platform's developers mapped language, responsiveness, the features that work well and the ones that cause friction, plus performance and the main bugs. The boards, one for White Label and one for the native apps, fed the scorecard and the comparison between solutions.

en.case.pefisa.tech.note: The technical analysis was carried out together with the Engineering team, considering criteria such as performance, bug identification, code quality, responsiveness and how the features work, to assess the technical quality of each solution and identify improvement opportunities.
en.case.pefisa.experience.title: Experience Analysis
en.case.pefisa.experience.desc: For each app, I gathered the store metrics (average rating, NPS and new insights) and the users' comments, grouped by theme (accounts, cards, financial and channels), to pinpoint the main pain points and improvement opportunities.

en.case.pefisa.features.desc: I mapped each app's features and crossed the four solutions in a single matrix, grouping equivalent features that appear under different names. The view makes clear what the digital accounts share, what is unique to each one and how much Pernambucanas leans on retail features.

en.case.pefisa.usability.title: Usability Analysis
en.case.pefisa.usability.desc: The four apps' usability was assessed against Nielsen's 10 heuristics, classic principles for spotting interface problems. Each feature got a 1–5 score on every heuristic, and the chart below compares each heuristic's average across the solutions.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h1.title: Visibility of system status
en.case.pefisa.usability.h1.desc: The system keeps users informed about what is going on, with clear and timely feedback.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h2.title: Match between system and the real world
en.case.pefisa.usability.h2.desc: It speaks the users’ language, with familiar words and concepts in a natural, logical order.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h3.title: User control and freedom
en.case.pefisa.usability.h3.desc: It offers clear exits to undo, go back or cancel an action taken by mistake.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h4.title: Consistency and standards
en.case.pefisa.usability.h4.desc: It behaves the same way throughout and follows platform conventions.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h5.title: Error prevention
en.case.pefisa.usability.h5.desc: It stops problems before they happen, with good defaults and confirmation before critical actions.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h6.title: Recognition rather than recall
en.case.pefisa.usability.h6.desc: Options and information stay visible, so users don’t have to remember things between screens.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h7.title: Flexibility and efficiency of use
en.case.pefisa.usability.h7.desc: It serves novices and experts alike, with shortcuts that speed up frequent tasks.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h8.title: Aesthetic and minimalist design
en.case.pefisa.usability.h8.desc: It shows only what matters for the task, with nothing competing with the essentials.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h9.title: Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors
en.case.pefisa.usability.h9.desc: Error messages in plain language that explain the problem and point to a fix.
en.case.pefisa.usability.h10.title: Help and documentation
en.case.pefisa.usability.h10.desc: When needed, help is easy to find and focused on the user’s task.

en.case.pefisa.strategy.p1: More than comparing screens, the analysis had to answer a business question: does it make sense to keep supporting two platforms to deliver the same product?
en.case.pefisa.strategy.p2: To answer it, I combined quantitative and qualitative metrics in a single framework. The main metrics collected were:
en.case.pefisa.strategy.p3: With them, I built a comparative scorecard (1 to 5 scale) crossing user value, business alignment, complexity reduction and financial return, which made it possible to identify the solution with the greatest potential for scale and centralization.
en.case.pefisa.strategy.item1: Performance: critical bug volume and average response time for each app.
en.case.pefisa.strategy.item2: Experience: average NPS per app and Google Play / App Store ratings.
en.case.pefisa.strategy.item3: Usability: assessment against the 10 heuristics and UX/UI Design patterns.
en.case.pefisa.strategy.p4: The final recommendation was to unify the solutions into a single application, built on the best-performing one and absorbing the relevant strengths of the others.
en.case.pefisa.strategy.p5: Unification brings lower costs, a simpler roadmap, greater technical efficiency and less effort spread across multiple codebases, increasing team efficiency and delivery speed.
en.case.pefisa.strategy.p6: The data gave the decision clarity and backed the proposal with concrete gains in cost, performance, user experience and scalability, strengthening Pefisa's digital strategy for the medium and long term.
en.case.pefisa.scorecard.label: Overall Assessment
en.case.pefisa.scorecard.intro: How the four digital accounts compare on the analysis' three pillars, Performance, Usability and Experience (1–5 scale).
en.case.pefisa.conclusion.title: Conclusion
en.case.pefisa.conclusion.p1: As a decision, Pernambucanas was set as the reference for the new product's technical architecture, thanks to its better performance and the chance to reuse its programming logic, reducing the complexity of the restructuring compared with the White Label solutions.
en.case.pefisa.conclusion.p2: For the user experience, Pefisa stood out for the specific features that broaden the digital account's value proposition, becoming a functional reference for the other products.
en.case.pefisa.conclusion.p3: Leroy Merlin, in turn, stood out as the reference for usability and visual consistency, with more uniform interface patterns and UX/UI best practices aimed at a more intuitive and efficient experience for customers.
en.case.pefisa.conclusion.p4: As the final deliverable of the analysis, a four-month roadmap was structured, covering the prioritized features, the first implementation phases and the plan for the new product's evolution. Given the project's high complexity, the chosen strategy was to start by building an MVP (Minimum Viable Product), evolving the solution incrementally until it reaches the technical and functional maturity needed to enable the full migration of the legacy.
en.case.pefisa.conclusion.p5: In this way, the strategy combines each solution's strengths: Pernambucanas' technology base, Pefisa's value features and Leroy Merlin's experience and usability patterns. The roadmap turns the analysis results into a structured execution plan, reducing implementation risks and guiding the progressive evolution toward a more efficient, consistent and scalable digital platform.
en.case.pefisa.impact.label: Estimated impact
en.case.pefisa.impact.intro: The unification strategy projects significant gains in cost, quality and experience, while increasing team efficiency and delivery speed.

en.case.pefisa.impact.metric2.desc: projected NPS points overall, with a consistent experience across brands
en.case.pefisa.impact.metric3.desc: fewer bugs through code consolidation and the end of redundant features
en.ds.introducao.p3: The library that shapes this portfolio. Patterns that were already spread across the pages (buttons, tags, cards, filters, toggles) were mapped, normalized into tokens and turned into components with documented variants, states and anatomy.
en.ds.introducao.p6: Playfair for emotion, Inter for reading. A neutral background and a single lime accent to guide the eye.
en.ds.introducao.p8: No loose hex codes: every color, size and duration comes from a variable that follows the theme.
en.ds.introducao.p10: Short transitions (150–300ms) confirm the interaction; nothing moves just for decoration.
en.ds.introducao.p12: Visible focus, AA contrast, semantic HTML and states that never rely on color alone.
en.ds.introducao.p16: Mapping of the patterns found on the site to the component that now represents them. The API follows shadcn/ui: one root class + variant and size modifiers.
en.ds.introducao.p60: Tokens live in src/index.css and components in src/components.css. Every playground has a Code tab with ready-to-copy HTML. Use Anatomy to see the parts and Measure to inspect size, padding and gap in px, read from the rendered component.
en.ds.introducao.li61: Values in the token tables are read live from the CSS, so they follow the light/dark theme.
en.ds.introducao.li62: Click any swatch, icon or token to copy it.
en.ds.cores.p3: A high-contrast palette with a single lime accent. Every color is a CSS variable redefined under [data-theme="light"]; switch the theme at the top to watch the values change.
en.ds.cores.p5: Background layers, from the page canvas to raised surfaces. The light section (--color-bg-light) creates the alternating rhythm of the home page.
en.ds.cores.p7: The badge shows the WCAG contrast on the matching background: AA ≥ 4.5, AA18 ≥ 3 (large text only).
en.ds.cores.p9: Lime is reserved for action and emphasis: primary CTA, focus, active state and markers. Text on the accent always uses --color-on-accent.
en.ds.cores.p11: System feedback. Each tone has a foreground + translucent background pair and always comes with an icon or text, never color alone.
en.ds.cores.p13: Transparency scale on top of the theme (white in dark, black in light) for borders, hovers and subtle surfaces.
en.ds.cores.li16: Use a single accent element per focus area.
en.ds.cores.li17: Pair semantic color with an icon and text.
en.ds.cores.li18: Reference tokens, never hex in the HTML.
en.ds.cores.li21: Accent as a body text color.
en.ds.tipografia.p3: Serif for headings with editorial personality; sans-serif for interface and long reading. Each row’s metadata is measured from the rendered text.
en.ds.espacamento.p3: A 4px-based scale aligned with the Tailwind classes already used on the site (p-6 = --space-6 = 24px).
en.ds.espacamento.p6: Content is capped at --container-max (1280px, max-w-7xl) with a --container-gutter gutter (24px, px-6). Layouts use a 12-column grid that collapses to one column below 768px.
en.ds.espacamento.li16: Sections: --space-24 on mobile, --space-32 on desktop (py-24 md:py-32).
en.ds.espacamento.li18: Related elements inside a card: --space-2 to --space-4.
en.ds.raios.p3: Soft rounding that grows with the element’s size. Interactive controls use pill; containers use md/lg.
en.ds.raios.p6: Nested elements use a smaller radius than their parent (inner radius ≈ outer radius − padding), avoiding “puffy” corners inside cards.
en.ds.elevacao.p3: In a dark theme, hierarchy comes more from translucent borders and surfaces than from shadows. Shadows signal floating or interaction.
en.ds.movimento.p3: Short durations with --ease-standard. The larger the element or the distance travelled, the longer the duration.
en.ds.movimento.li10: With prefers-reduced-motion, transitions and pulses are turned off.
en.ds.iconografia.p3: Tabler Icons (webfont), 2px stroke, consistent with Inter’s weight. Icons inherit text color and size.
en.ds.iconografia.p10: Click to copy the HTML. Decorative icons get aria-hidden="true"; icon-only buttons need an aria-label on the button.
en.ds.button.p3: Triggers an action or navigation. Five variants in decreasing emphasis, three sizes and an optional icon on the left, the right or on its own.
en.ds.button.li19: Minimum height of 36px (sm); md and lg meet the 44px touch target.
en.ds.button.li20: 2px accent focus ring with a 2px offset, shown for keyboard only (:focus-visible).
en.ds.button.li21: Loading uses aria-busy="true" and blocks double clicks.
en.ds.badge.p3: A short, non-interactive label to classify or show state. It unifies the skill tags, the case section labels and the semantic status pills.
en.ds.badge.li17: Status with an icon so it doesn’t rely on color.
en.ds.badge.li19: Using a badge as a button; to filter, use a Chip.
en.ds.badge.li20: Mixing variants in the same group.
en.ds.chip.p3: Toggle button for filters (Pefisa feature table and dashboard). Click the chip in the preview to toggle its state.
en.ds.chip.li7: A chip is a <button> with aria-pressed; screen readers announce “pressed”.
en.ds.chip.li8: Group chips in a container with role="group" and an aria-label (“Filter by platform”).
en.ds.chip.li9: For a single choice between options, prefer the Segmented Control.
en.ds.segmented.p3: Switches between mutually exclusive views of the same content, like App/Web in the galleries or Dark/Light in the styleguide. Try it with clicks and arrow keys.
en.ds.segmented.li8: Roving tabindex: Tab lands on the selected item; arrows move the selection.
en.ds.segmented.li9: 2 to 4 options. Beyond that, use tabs or a select.
en.ds.input.p3: Text field with an always-visible label, optional icon and a helper or error message. Origin: the Profile sign-in form.
en.ds.input.li8: Label outside the field, linked with for/id.
en.ds.input.li13: Showing an error with a red border only.
en.ds.card.p3: Groups related content. Three variants from the home page and the cases: Lead (skills), Case (project showcase) and Metric (results).
en.ds.card.li7: A case card is a single <a>: the whole area is clickable and screen readers read the content once.
en.ds.card.li8: In grids, keep the same variant and equal heights (align-items: stretch).
en.ds.card.li9: Metrics: a short number (≤ 5 characters) + a one-line description.
en.ds.accordion.p3: A list of expandable sections, used for Nielsen’s heuristics in the Pefisa case. Built on <details>, no JavaScript.
en.ds.accordion.li7: <summary> is already focusable and responds to Enter/Space; the open state is announced natively.
en.ds.accordion.li8: Content stays findable with the browser’s find-in-page.
en.ds.tooltip.p3: A bubble with supplementary information, shown on hover and focus. It standardizes the chart tooltips (scorecard, radar, bars).
en.ds.tooltip.li11: Hiding essential information only in the tooltip.
en.ds.tooltip.li12: Links or buttons inside the bubble.
en.ds.navbar.p3: A fixed frosted-glass header present on every page. Made of the logo, section links and actions (theme, social, contact).
en.ds.navbar.li7: position: fixed with backdrop-filter: blur(16px); content scrolls underneath and stays legible.
en.ds.navbar.li8: Below 768px the links hide and only the actions remain.
